newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ERM membership -- is it really necessary for EMU?.
newsitem.headline: ERM membership -- is it really necessary for EMU?.

text.p: The controversial issue of whether membership in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism is mandatory for those wishing to join a single currency resurfaced on Monday after Britain said participation was not necessary.

In his first outing with EU finance ministers, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Gordon Brown, responded with an unequivocal "no" when asked whether he believed participation in the ERM was required if Britain wanted to join the euro.
The vexed question was further muddied by Dutch finance minister Gerrit Zalm who said memberhsip was open to interpretation.
"There is some difference of interpretation among lawyers," Zalm told reporters.
At the same ministerial gathering German Finance Minister Theo Waigel reiterated his position that any country wishing to join a single currency must be a member of the ERM.
The confusion stems primarily from the fact that the ERM underwent a severe crisis in 1992, leading to a widening of the trading bands for participating currencies from 2.25 percent to 15 percent.

Since the event, those opposed to mandatory ERM membership have argued that the Maastricht treaty's precondition was no longer relevant and that currency stability -- the original intention of ERM inclusion -- could be demonstrated outside the currency grid.
But for those who believe the criterion is still valid, such as Germany, the overriding view is that membership leads to greater stability, 15 percent bands notwithstanding.
Taking its cue from this hardline stance, Italy rejoined the ERM last autumn in an effort to enhance its credentials for joining economic and monetary union in 1999.
Both Italy and Britain were ejected from the ERM in 1992, an event which has left British politicans of all stripes adamantly opposed to going back in.

A strict reading of the criterion, however, would lead to Italy's disqualification. Specifically, the treaty says a country must be an ERM participant two years prior to the decision on which countries join EMU.
Since that judgment will be made next spring, Italy will technically fall short of the deadline.
More realistically, there are those who argue that membership is not that important provided a country fulfils all the other Maastricht criteria on inflation, deficits and debt.
In the event that Britain wanted to actually join the euro in 1999, and met all of the other requirements, some EU officials say it would be politically difficult to keep them out.
